query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC HEA multilayer coatings, the presence of semicoherent interfaces (as in the 16 nm modulation period multilayer) leads to localized stress-induced interfacial amorphization under sustained nanoindentation loading. This amorphization, driven by dislocation pileup at misfit dislocations, lowers atomic-migration barriers and transitions the deformation mechanism from dislocation-mediated creep to diffusion/interface-slip-mediated creep, resulting in enhanced creep resistance compared to multilayers with coherent interfaces (8 nm) or grain-boundary-dominated structures (32/80 nm).
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, approximately 1 μm-thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings produced from Al0.2CrFeNi and Al targets.
generation.intervention: Modulation period (λ) variation via RF magnetron sputtering to produce multilayers with 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm layer thicknesses, establishing coherent (M8), semicoherent (M16), and grain-boundary-dominated (M32 and M80) interfaces, followed by room-temperature nanoindentation creep testing.
generation.conditions: Deposition conditions include a base pressure of ~5×10^-4 Pa, 100 sccm Ar, 0.3 Pa working pressure, and specified target powers and deposition time; room-temperature nanoindentation with a 5 mN maximum load, varying loading rates (1, 0.1, 0.01 mN/s), a 100 s hold, and 20 s unloading, with indentation depths around 1/10–1/7 of the coating thickness.
generation.structural_mediator: Interface coherency. In the semicoherent M16 multilayer, misfit dislocations at the FCC/BCC boundaries promote localized stress buildup that leads to interfacial amorphization.
generation.mechanism: The semicoherent interfaces block dislocation glide, causing dislocation pileup and localized high stresses that induce amorphization at the interface. This amorphous interfacial phase has increased free volume and disorder, which lowers the barriers for atomic diffusion or interface slip. Consequently, the deformation mechanism shifts from dislocation-mediated creep (typical in coherent or grain-boundary-dominated interfaces) to a diffusion/interface-slip-mediated creep, delaying plastic deformation under sustained loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: The 16 nm semicoherent multilayer (M16) will exhibit the highest room-temperature creep resistance with a measured creep stress exponent (n) trending lower (around values characteristic of diffusion/interface-slip, i.e., approximately 1–2) compared to the higher values (n > 3) observed in coherent (M8) and grain-boundary-dominated (M32/M80) multilayers.
generation.baseline: Comparisons with M8 (8 nm, featuring coherent interfaces that transmit dislocations easily) and M32/M80 (32/80 nm, dominated by grain boundaries and undergoing primarily dislocation-mediated creep) where the typical creep behavior is governed by dislocation slip or climb.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is limited to the as-deposited ~1 μm thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer coatings under room-temperature conditions as tested by nanoindentation creep with estimated loading rates and indentation depths specified; extrapolation to elevated temperatures or different scales of deformation requires further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism of stress-induced amorphization is supported by prior MD/HRTEM studies, the precise kinetics of the amorphization process and its quantitative impact on reducing migration barriers remain uncertain and require further precise measurement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multilayers with identical overall composition and thickness but with modulation periods of 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm. Characterize the interface types using XRD and TEM (including IFFT analysis) to confirm coherent, semicoherent, and grain-boundary-dominated interfaces. Perform room-temperature nanoindentation creep tests at varying loading rates (1, 0.1, 0.01 mN/s) and hold times. Analyze load–displacement curves and measure displacement versus dwell time to calculate the creep strain rate and determine the creep stress exponent (n) using ln(strain rate) versus ln(flow stress) plots.
measurements: XRD and TEM/IFFT to characterize interface structures and confirm presence of misfit dislocations or amorphous interfacial regions.
Nanoindentation load–displacement curves and displacement–time data to extract creep strain rates.
Determination of the creep stress exponent (n) from ln(strain rate) vs ln(flow stress) analysis, distinguishing diffusion/interface-slip creep (n ~ 1–2) from dislocation-mediated creep (n > 3).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 16 nm multilayer does not show a significant shift in the creep mechanism (i.e., if its creep stress exponent does not trend towards lower values, or if no signs of stress-induced interfacial amorphization are observed) compared to the coherent (8 nm) and grain-boundary-dominated (32/80 nm) multilayers, then the hypothesis is rejected.
